nutshell: Person search (joint detection + re-ID) methods typically share a backbone between the two sub-tasks, causing conflicting gradients, and rely on ImageNet-pretrained backbones that are weak at capturing fine-grained, multi-person spatial context. DiffPS instead uses a frozen pretrained text-to-image diffusion model (Stable Diffusion v2-1's UNet) as the backbone, extracting separate task-specific features for detection and re-ID from its internal representations without any fine-tuning, fully eliminating the shared-backbone optimization conflict.
contributions: First use of a frozen pretrained diffusion model's internal UNet features as the backbone for person search, completely decoupling detection and re-ID optimization since the backbone is never updated - verified in Table 2, where DiffPS gets identical performance whether the two tasks are trained jointly or separately, unlike prior 'decoupled' methods (DMRNet/DMRNet++) that still update a shared backbone and show real performance drops under joint optimization.

Diffusion-Guided Region Proposal Network (DGRPN): thresholds the 'person'-token cross-attention map into confidence peaks, builds Gaussian maps around each peak with locally-estimated variance, and uses this to modulate the detection feature map before a standard RPN - using text-image attention alignment as a person-localization prior.

Multi-Scale Frequency Refinement Network (MSFRN): a hierarchical Discrete Wavelet Transform-based refinement over 7 multi-scale up-stage feature maps, specifically designed to counteract diffusion features' 'shape bias' (low-frequency/global-structure dominance from the denoising process) by re-emphasizing high-frequency sub-bands needed for fine-grained identity discrimination.

Semantic-adaptive Feature Aggregation Network (SFAN): exploits the diffusion model's CLIP text-image alignment by computing cosine similarity between refined features and fixed body-part text prompts ('head'/'shirts'/'pants'/'shoes'), then aggregates the resulting spatial semantic maps with learnable per-part weights into the final person representation.
New SOTA on CUHK-SYSU (97.8 mAP / 98.4 Top-1) and PRW (62.0 mAP / 91.0 Top-1), outperforming ResNet50/ConvNeXt/PVTv2/Swin-S-backbone prior methods.
deficiencies: The backbone comparison isn't compute-matched: DiffPS swaps in a full Stable Diffusion v2-1 UNet (pretrained on LAION-5B, far larger than ResNet50/ConvNeXt/PVTv2/Swin-S) as a frozen feature extractor, but the paper never reports parameter count, FLOPs, or inference latency for the full pipeline versus the compared methods - a real cost given diffusion UNets are typically much heavier than the CNN/ViT backbones being outperformed.

The feature-selection ablation (Table 3) is somewhat inconsistent: the chosen best configuration (g, Level 1+2+3) wins on mAP (62.0) by only 0.7 over the runner-up (f, Level 2+3, 61.3 mAP), but (f) actually has the higher Top-1 accuracy (91.2 vs. 91.0) - the paper picks (g) as 'optimal' without discussing this metric disagreement.

Margins over the strongest prior baseline (SEAS w/ ConvNeXt) are fairly small - +0.7 mAP on CUHK-SYSU (97.8 vs. 97.1) and +1.5 mAP on PRW (62.0 vs. 60.5) - and on PRW Top-1, DiffPS (91.0) is actually below SeqNeXt+GFN (92.4); the text notes this in one sentence without discussing why a diffusion-prior backbone would specifically underperform a ConvNeXt gallery-filtering method on Top-1.
All results are on only two datasets (CUHK-SYSU, PRW) with single-run numbers and no variance/seed reporting, despite some claimed improvements being under 1 mAP point.
notable: The timestep analysis (Fig. 5, Sec. 4.3) finds both detection and re-ID perform best at t=0 (no added diffusion noise at all) - notably different from prior diffusion-feature literature (cited in the paper's own related work) which recommends moderate timesteps (e.g. t~300) for simpler, less cluttered images; the paper attributes this to person-search scenes already being visually complex before any synthetic noise is added. Worth flagging for anyone porting 'typical' diffusion-feature-extraction timestep advice to a new, more cluttered domain. DGRPN's Gaussian-map construction from thresholded attention peaks (Eq. 1-4) is also a lightweight, trainable-parameter-light way to convert a noisy cross-attention heatmap into smooth region proposals without a separately trained detector head.
